A man was shot inside the city subway system in Midtown Saturday afternoon, police said.
The NYPD confirmed the shooting took place near the 53rd Street and 7th Avenue station, which serves the B, D and E lines, but released no other details. It’s unclear if the shooting took place aboard a train or in the station and if there were other victims.
Also unclear is the condition of the man who was shot.
The MTA had no information on the incident.
Uptown E trains were running on the F line between West 4th Street–Washington Square and Jackson Heights–Roosevelt Avenue, and uptown D trains were bypassing the station while police investigated, according to MTA service alerts.
As of Oct. 11, four people have been shot in the transit system this year, up from two over the same period in 2025, according to statistics from the NYPD.
This is a developing story based on preliminary police information and will be updated.

The NYPD is hoping you can help bring a very good girl home to Queens.
Chanel, a 10-year-old Yorkshire Terrier, was frolicking on her front lawn near 130th Street and 14th Avenue in College Point when she was abducted, police said. Two people in a 2014 Subaru Forester pulled up to the home, one of them scooped up Chanel and then both dognappers sped off, according to the NYPD.
The abduction was late last month, but as of this weekend, police are still searching for Chanel.
Earlier this week, the NYPD released her photo to help in the search. She’s a tiny tan-and-silver Yorkie and looks a bit like a teddy bear.
Police are investigating the incident as a grand larceny and said the dog is valued — as if you can put a value on a dog’s life — at $1,200.
Anyone with information that could help reunite Chanel and her owner is asked to call the NYPD’s Crime Stoppers Hotline at 1-800-577-TIPS (8477).

articles.title: Being reigning champions is weird for Knicks fans, but we could get used to this.
articles.text:
Being reigning champions is weird for Knicks fans, but we could get used to this. - Gothamist
News
Being reigning champions is weird for Knicks fans, but we could get used to this.
By
Catalina Gonella
Published Oct 17, 2026 at 10:00 a.m. ET
Share

Photo by Roy Rochlin/Getty Images
By
Catalina Gonella
Published Oct 17, 2026 at 10:00 a.m. ET
Share

Enduring disappointment and heartbreak, staying loyal through shame and misery, and fanning the flames of hope had all become as much a part of being a die-hard New York Knicks fan as wearing orange and blue … and maybe hating Knicks owner James Dolan.
Then NYC’s hometown team won the 2026 NBA Championship.
The New York Knicks will raise their first championship banner at Madison Square Garden in 50 years as they open their season on Tuesday night. And fans, still riding the high of the team's ultimate win, are slowly getting used to cheering for defending champions.
“I had like a little moment of, ‘Oh no, like, what about my identity as a Knicks fan? We're supposed to suck, and I'm supposed to be miserable about it,’” said lifelong fan and Connecticut native Zach Rudes, 41, who watched last season’s final game in the middle of the night where he now lives in Spain. “I think being a fan of a perpetually cursed team kind of became part of my identity.”
Being a Knicks fan, he said, was “very Murphy's Law.”
Manhattan resident Daniel Barth, 30, was glad to shake off the sense of misfortune associated with the fandom.
“I feel a sense of relief to just kind of let go of that suffering,” Barth said. “To see them finally get over that hump and achieve the championship success, which I have wanted to see for this team for years, is just such a gratifying experience. It's like a healing experience.”
Fans cheer during the New York Knicks Championship ticker tape parade and victory rally June 7.
Michael Nigro/Pacific Press/LightRocket via Getty Images
Before this summer, the Knicks hadn’t won a championship since 1973. There had been some glimmers of hope — like when they made it to the finals in 1994 and 1999. Or in the 2010s, when the team acquired All-Star Carmelo Anthony. Then, when basketball executive Leon Rose was hired as team president in 2020, the Knicks really began to shape up.
“I think that's when that winning culture started and like that's when we got into the habit of actually winning consistently year after year,” said Queens native Donté Ledbetter. “I think that's what a lot of Knicks fans want to see. … I mean, it's quite embarrassing every time you bring up the Knicks; at least in the past, people would be like ‘Oh sorry.’ But now we're not a laughingstock anymore.”
Knicks fans had the last laugh this June. Captain Jalen Brunson and the team achieved what fans had dreamed of for 53 years — in Game 4 of the finals against the San Antonio Spurs, the Knicks completed the largest comeback in NBA Finals history. In Game 5, they sealed the deal.
Tens of thousands of fans spilled out onto the streets around Madison Square Garden. Dense crowds stretched from Fifth to Ninth avenues. The city erupted in a cacophony of shouts, fireworks, car horns, music and jubilant chants of "Knicks in five!”
For many diehard fans, years spent in the trenches with their team made the win that much sweeter — a feeling that will be hard to beat.
“I genuinely, I never thought I was gonna see it, honestly,” Bronx resident Brian Brennan said.
“This was the year where everything changed for me as a Knicks fan. The past pain, the heartbreak, the bad seasons, the brutal playoff losses — that made it worth it to go through that, and to go through those scars, to get those scars, to come out on top, and to finally be able to say that we have that, really made it even more special for me.”
The New York Knicks celebrate during the Championship ticker tape parade and victory rally.
Angelina Katsanis/Getty Images
New York City had become one giant watch party. What had once been a tortured club of basketball fanatics had gone mainstream. Everyone was a Knicks fan. Times were changing.
“I think that a part of me almost has this melancholy to a former time where there was a really tight-knit community of Knicks fans,” 34-year-old New Jerseyan Patrick Conor said. “But on the other end of things, it's so wonderful to see a whole new generation of fans being born through the championship, through the playoff runs, and that they get different experiences.”
With the start of the new season, New York Knicks fans are cautiously optimistic, if not wary, of the team's future, especially because of Dolan's leadership. He’d long been criticized for the team’s previous decades of poor performance (not to mention his surveillance of fans and politicians at MSG, and high ticket prices). His latest infractions, according to fans, involve not wanting to shell out the cash it would have cost to keep key player Mitchell Robinson. Karl-Anthony Towns’ future also remains uncertain, with reports that his contract negotiations with the team are at a standstill.
“We're still like a little anxious and paranoid, you know what I mean? Like gun-shy that it's all gonna collapse,” longtime loyal fan Keif Roberts said. “A lot of Knicks fans, myself included, are a little bit wary of what direction we're gonna go now.  I know that James Dolan doesn't wanna get into the second apron [a penalty for spending above the NBA salary cap], and that he's been talking about that.”

The parks committee of an East Village community board has backed a plan to renovate the basketball courts, a kids-only swimming pool, and a beloved '90s-era outdoor fitness area in Tompkins Square Park. Some miffed park users say the effort goes too far.
Many Tompkins Square regulars, including a handful who told Gothamist their lives revolve around the park’s steel pull-up bars, have panned the renovation plans. In the East Village’s latest preservation fight, more than 2,600 people signed a petition urging the city “not to ‘fix’ what is not broken.”
“ There's no reason to change this particular fitness area because we love it the way it is,” said Danny Kavadlo, a personal trainer who said he has been training in Tompkins Square Park for more than 15 years.
A look at some of the "no frills" recreation offerings in Tompkins Square Park in the East Village.
Willow Higgins/Gothamist
The parks department presented three different proposals to the community board’s committee on Thursday night. One option left the fitness area undisturbed – a route that park preservationists said would have been a victory.
Much to their dismay, the community board committee agreed with the recommendation of the parks department, which said the entire area should be renovated, including the outdoor gym.
The committee will bring its resolution to the full community board at its next meeting.
The parks department said the new fitness equipment would be safer, accessible to people with disabilities, and that the aging equipment has to be updated anyway. The project has nearly $10 million in funding from the mayor and governor, according to the parks department presentation.
Proponents of keeping the park as is, however, told Gothamist the fight is far from over and they plan to make their voices heard.
A look at some of the "no frills" recreation offerings in Tompkins Square Park in the East Village.
Willow Higgins/Gothamist
“To be clear we are not arguing that nothing ever needs repair,” Salo Coslovsky, an associate professor of urban planning at New York University at the forefront of the preservation fight, said in a statement. “We are arguing that Parks is misrepresenting the status of the park and using repairable problems to justify a much larger, more disruptive reconstruction.”
The plan that the community board committee opted to support includes building a new, in-ground miniature pool for kids with improved infrastructure. The city would put detention basins under the renovated basketball court to improve storm runoff and prevent sewage from flowing into the East River.
A look at some of the "no frills" recreation offerings in Tompkins Square Park in the East Village.
Willow Higgins/Gothamist
The fitness equipment would be replaced with new materials to make it safer and more accessible, according to the parks department. While the original plan proposed eliminating the half basketball court in the area, the committee requested it be preserved.
Jonathan Fodi, an electrical engineer, said he moved to the East Village from Montreal after visiting his cousin who lived in the area. He said he was awestruck when he first saw the park’s community.
“People are doing handstands on the bars. People are hanging. There's music,” Fodi said. “ There was guys of all different races, ages, doesn't really matter. I was like, ‘This place is awesome,’ and it's what made me wanna move here.”
Now, he said, he’s made more friends than he can count at the park.
Lifelong East Village residents rely on the space, too.
Jahmal Kirwan said he grew up just blocks away. He said the park hasn't just helped him get into shape, it’s also helped stop drinking, stay out of trouble, and connect to his community.
Kirwan said he can’t think of anywhere nearby that would be an adequate replacement during construction, which the parks department said is expected to take 18 months.
“ It forces us to have nowhere to go,” he said. “Back to the block, basically, you know? Back to the trenches.”
At the meeting, representatives from the parks department said they are learning from past mistakes and appreciate the community feedback.
The department said it is speaking with different manufacturers about obtaining higher-quality materials to use for the renovation, as other park improvement projects have yielded complaints.
The department also said that the proposed design would have the same features as the current one, in addition to accessible equipment and layout.
“In order to invest in the care of our parks, we must regularly redesign and rebuild our city’s parks and facilities,” the department’s website reads.
But the park preservationists insist they won’t give up without a fight. Coslovsky said he will be at the next community board meeting with more specific requests, including increasing the accessibility and repairing existing equipment in a way that is minimally disruptive to an “epicenter of wellbeing, affordability, friendship and community.”
Kerwin and Fodi said they are planning a park party to give people a sense of the type of community it fosters.
“There's a certain energy that these bars have and a certain type of people that it attracts,” Fodi said. “The biggest thing about this place is the people.”

Watch out New Jersey drivers: Environmental officials warn lustful deer seeking sex are a major hazard on Garden State roads this fall.
The state’s Department of Environmental Protection issued a notice Friday noting it’s peak mating season for white-tailed deer, which means the creatures “are more likely to be present near and on roadways as bucks attempt to court does.”
New Jersey deer are expected to keep seeking action through mid-December, and officials say drivers should be on high alert, especially after daylight savings time ends on Nov. 1, causing commutes to more closely align with deer activity. About 77% of deer crashes occur during the evening rush, state officials said.
According to State Farm Insurance data, Garden State drivers have a one in 226 chance of an animal collision. October through December account for about 41% of all those crashes, with November seeing the highest share.
“Collisions with deer pose a very serious safety threat and can cause significant damage to vehicles and possible loss of life,” David Golden, assistant commissioner of the Division of Fish and Wildlife under the state Department of Environmental Protection, wrote in a statement.
It can cost an average of around $4,000 to repair car damage caused by a deer strike, according to Purdue University, but a collision can also total a vehicle.
New Jersey officials urged drivers to exercise caution by driving slower, using high beams, keeping an eye out for deer and minding deer-crossing signs. They warn that if you see one deer, there are likely more nearby.
New Jersey's deer population exceeds 100,000. According to the New Jersey Conservation Foundation, deer numbers are in many areas are 10 times above healthy levels and are fueling an ecological crisis as well as endangering public health and safety.
“It’s especially important that drivers be extra vigilant to this threat and take time to know steps that can be taken to reduce the risk of collision,” Golden said.

Prosecutors say a man accused of poisoning two female college students with fentanyl and raping one of them in a Manhattan dorm room messaged a friend a week earlier that a sample of the drugs had made him sick and that he had “straight poison,” according to court records.
Federal prosecutors accused Moises Freire of giving two women a substance that he claimed was “pure cocaine” but was actually fentanyl, causing them both to lose consciousness. Freire then raped one of the women, according to the indictment. The U.S. attorney’s office said one woman survived, while the other died days later in a hospital. Prosecutors did not name either woman in charging papers.
A federal grand jury indicted Freire and Brian Peralta Cabrera on various drug-related charges Thursday. Prosecutors accused Peralta Cabrera of providing the drugs to Freire.
The charges come amid outcry over sexual violence on college campuses, after a former Cornell University student alleged in a bombshell lawsuit that she was gang raped at the Ivy League college in Upstate New York.
The indictment does not name the Manhattan university where the incident allegedly occurred, but Freire’s attorney said at a past court hearing that it happened at the Fashion Institute of Technology in Chelsea, which is part of the state university system.
A school spokesperson did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Defense attorneys for Freire and Peralta Cabrera also did not immediately respond to questions.
Prosecutors initially charged Freire, Peralta Cabrera and another man with conspiring to distribute narcotics that resulted in death and serious bodily injury this past spring. They all pleaded not guilty at the time.
A transcript of a federal court hearing in April reveals new details about what prosecutors and defense attorneys say happened, based on messages and video footage.
Assistant U.S. Attorney Ariana Bloom told the judge that Freire tricked the two women into thinking the drugs were cocaine, telling lies that the substance was “pure” and purchased from a trusted source on a recent trip to Mexico.
She said that when Freire, who was 18 at the time, tested the drugs a week before, he messaged a friend that he felt lightheaded, was trembling and felt like he was going to vomit.
"I got straight poison,” Freire told his friend, according to the prosecutor.
His friend, whom the attorneys did not name, responded that he shouldn’t take the drugs himself and should give it to the “sluts,” Bloom said at the hearing. “Disturbingly, the defendant did exactly that,” she told U.S. District Judge Sidney H. Stein.
On March 18, she said, Freire pressured the women to use the drugs and didn’t take them himself. Freire admitted in a statement to campus security that he had been having sex with one of the women and realized she was unconscious when he opened his eyes afterward, according to Bloom.
He then looked to his left and saw the other woman on the floor with her eyes rolled back in her head, the prosecutor said he told campus police.
Bloom said Freire texted his friends that the women were unconscious and sent multiple photos of them while they were passed out. She said Freire waited at least 40 minutes to get help, and that the drugs had disappeared by the time law enforcement searched the room.
“So it's unclear what the defendant was doing in those 40 minutes other than sending text messages to his friends and not calling for help,” the prosecutor said. “So all of that suggests that the defendant not only knowingly brought a dangerous substance to a college dorm and pressured two college girls to use it, but then once things started going south, instead of calling 9-1-1 or alerting someone or prioritizing their lives, he took time to take pictures of them and to protect himself.”
Freire’s attorney, federal defender Mitchell Schwartz, said at the April court hearing that his client was not a student at FIT but had been accepted to John Jay College of Criminal Justice and needed to complete an internship before he started classes.
He said Freire and the woman who died had known each other for about a year and had been in some sort of relationship, starting when he was in high school and she was in college.
Schwartz said his client is not a drug dealer and that the women were the ones who invited him over and asked him to bring cocaine. He called what happened “a tragedy” but denied that his client is “some evil kid.”
After reading and listening to messages between Freire and the woman in the lead-up to her death, he said it was “like I would say reading a story of teenagers doing what I would call dumb teenager things.”
“It’s not dumb teenager things to give somebody fentanyl, sir,” the judge responded.
In April, Stein ordered that Freire be held in jail without bail until his trial.
“The proof in court, the proof is extremely strong,” the judge said.
A court date has not yet been set for Freire and Peralta Cabrera to be arraigned on the new charges.

The effort to redevelop a Midtown high rise after a near-catastrophic structural failure is now underway — a hair’s breadth at a time.
Newly filed engineering plans for the city’s largest office-to-housing conversion project show construction crews will gradually jack up sagging floors in increments of 1/64th of an inch, or roughly the size of the edge of a business card. They will eventually raise the floors about 7 inches.
The work is set to begin more than three months after city officials said they were concerned the so-called Pfizer Building at 235 East 42nd St. would collapse when a pair of columns on the 21st floor folded beneath a major expansion of the existing structure. As Gothamist first reported, the columns were not reinforced despite an engineer’s city-approved instructions to turn the flimsy I-shaped beams into sturdy boxes.
Immediately after the debacle, project developer MetroLoft described plans to rebuild the section of the tower where the columns bent. The company’s strategy has now changed, according to the engineering plans and reviews submitted to the Department of Buildings.
A MetroLoft spokesperson declined to comment on the project or new strategy.
A spokesperson for the engineering firm Thornton Tomasetti, which drafted the plan, also declined to comment. The company has handled other major projects around the city, including the arch at Grand Army Plaza and a 70-story apartment complex called the Orchard in Long Island City.
Another firm, Plan B Engineering, reviewed the project plan and submitted its analysis to the Department of Buildings. The company did not respond to phone calls seeking comment.
FDNY drone imagery shows a buckled steel structural member inside the office-to-residential conversion project at 235 E. 42nd St., where officials say two structural columns failed and floors above began to sag. Courtesy of FDNY.
Some work was already underway on the higher floors of the project when Gothamist visited Friday, with a hoist elevator seen moving up and down the side of the building near the site of the collapsed columns. Records show the columns were removed last month and Department of Buildings spokesperson David Maggiotto said the jacking is scheduled to begin next week.
The city’s Department of Buildings has not yet released the results of an investigation into the cause of the near-disaster.
Maggiotto said the new project plan is safe and that agency engineers will oversee the work.
“We would not allow any work to proceed in the city if we thought it was posing a hazard to the public,” Maggiotto said. “These plans to effectuate permanent structural repairs to the building were approved by DOB following an extensive vetting and review process by senior department engineers, as well as from an independent third-party engineering firm.”
The new plans were first reported by the New York Times.
The company Barone Steel Fabricators was hired to handle initial steel installation, according to job filings. Following the July incident, the city’s Department of Buildings targeted other projects handled by Barone in a citywide safety enforcement sweep, Gothamist previously reported.
Barone executives did not respond to requests for comment on the project. An attorney for the company, Paul Callan, told Gothamist that Barone is no longer working on the job after it “completed all required work under the contract to date."
“They are not working on the job site now but may be back to complete other contracted work,” Callan said Friday. "They have not been fired, they have not been terminated.”
Callan said that “there’s been no criticism” of Barone.
A framing plan for the 20th and 21st floors of the office-to-housing conversion at 235 East 42nd St.
New York City Department of Buildings
The proposed 1,600-unit apartment complex is set to be the city’s largest-ever office-to-housing conversion project. But the structural failure at the building that once housed the headquarters of the pharmaceutical giant Pfizer prompted a flurry of concern over similar projects across the five boroughs. City leaders, including Mayor Zohran Mamdani, have embraced office conversions as the fastest way to increase the amount of housing in New York City.
After the Pfizer Building incident, the Department of Buildings said it conducted an analysis of other office conversion projects and did not find problems.
Structural engineers who reviewed the new plans to gradually jack up the floors said MetroLoft’s revised strategy appeared safe and incremental.
“The threat is going too fast and missing a problem, like something that is causing damage somewhere else,” said Eric Cowley, president of the firm Cowley Engineering.
Cowley said he did not see a need to redevelop the entire section of the building above the bent columns, despite MetroLoft’s initial pronouncements.
"I think the repair is fine,” he said. “It’s not cost-effective to rebuild unless that were changing the configuration or adding volume.”
Structural engineer Abi Aghayere, a professor at Drexel University, said he saw “nothing unusual” in the peer-reviewed plan to begin jacking a fraction of an inch at a time.
“It’s testing the system,” Aghayere said. “They want to make sure everything is safe.”

A city investigation published Thursday found a yellow bus carrying six nonverbal autistic students in Brooklyn was lost for more than four hours on the way to school last year while a panicked group of parents and school officials struggled to locate the children.
The report by the Special Commissioner of Investigation, a watchdog agency for the city’s public schools, said a bus operated by Consolidated Bus Transit was scheduled to arrive at a Brooklyn elementary school before 9 a.m. on Dec. 16, but did not show up until 1:25 p.m. that day.
Parents tried to track the bus’s winding route via AirTags placed in their children’s backpacks while school staff struggled to reach the bus company, the investigation found. When the bus of 6- to 8-year-olds did arrive, one student was lying in a pool of urine, according to the report.
It’s the latest in a string of incidents that have parents and regulators calling for urgent reforms to the city’s dysfunctional school bus system. While the majority of New York’s students walk, drive or take public transit to school, about 155,000 rely on yellow buses. Half of those using the buses have disabilities.
Parents have long complained of delays, circuitous routes, broken GPS systems and unresponsive call center staff. They said improving the bus system will require passing legislation in Albany so the city can rebid and replace 45-year-old bus contracts with new contracts that add strict requirements for vendors and strengthen service for students.
“It is highly disturbing that six nonverbal children were left on a school bus for hours while their whereabouts remained unknown to school officials,” Special Commissioner Anastasia Coleman said in a statement. “These particularly vulnerable students rely on the adults entrusted with their care to ensure their safety.”
According to the report, the bus driver said he stopped at two incorrect addresses before the bus company called with a correct address for P.S. 289 in Crown Heights. The driver and attendant were both fill-ins temporarily assigned to the route, and the bus’s GPS system was “inoperable,” the report said. During the four hours when the bus was missing, worried school staff filed a police report.
Representatives for the bus company did not immediately respond to requests for comment.
Education department officials said the bus driver and attendant were immediately suspended. The special commissioner of investigation’s office recommended that the two employees never be allowed to supervise city public school children going forward.
At the start of the school year, thousands of students who needed buses to get to school did not have access to them. Education department officials said an ongoing driver shortage has been exacerbated by an increase in the number of children with disabilities who need busing.
Mayor Zohran Mamdani has said his administration is working to address both the immediate and structural problems with the bus system.
“We are doing everything we can to ensure that every single student is able to get to school,” Mamdani said at a press conference on the first day of school. “And we are also working at addressing this long-term issue.”
